subtopics.name: Frequency counting & anagrams
subtopics.summary: Count occurrences of each character (array of 26 or a map) and reason only about the multiset of letters. Appears whenever order does not matter: anagrams, rearrangements into palindromes, "can we make the strings equal by swaps", distinct-character splits.
learn: Use int cnt[26] (c - 'a') instead of map<char,int> for speed and simplicity
Two strings are anagrams iff their count arrays are equal; rearrangement questions reduce to comparing counts
Prefix/suffix distinct counts let you evaluate every split point in O(n * 26) or O(n)
A multiset can be arranged into a palindrome iff at most one letter has an odd count
Map one string to another (pattern templates) with two maps to enforce a bijection
Pitfall: uppercase/lowercase and digits need separate offsets; reset count arrays between test cases in O(26), not O(maxn)

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Sets & Maps

subtopics.name: Runs, blocks & binary strings
subtopics.summary: Split a string into maximal blocks of equal characters (run-length encoding) and reason about the number of blocks, their lengths and the transitions between them. Very common in 800-1700 problems on binary strings: deleting/merging blocks, counting "01"/"10" boundaries, cutting a string into pieces, games that remove blocks.
learn: Run-length encode in one pass: vector of (char, length); the number of blocks = 1 + number of i with s[i] != s[i-1]
Many operations only change block counts by at most 1 or 2: think in terms of boundaries (transitions), not characters
Binary string sortedness: a sorted 0...01...1 string has at most one "10" boundary; count "10" transitions to measure distance from sorted
Games removing blocks: players greedily take the largest remaining block of 1s (sort block lengths)
Substring counting by the last transition: any substring ending at i whose last two characters differ behaves like the whole prefix (Paranoid String pattern)
Cyclic strings: rotate so the string starts at a block boundary, then merge the first and last block if equal
Greedy with a pointer over blocks: delete from the earliest block of length >= 2 to save operations

subtopics.name: Palindromes (basic)
subtopics.summary: Recognise and construct palindromes with two pointers from both ends and mirrored positions i and n-1-i. Typical tasks: make a string a palindrome with minimum changes, build the longest palindrome from given pieces, decide if some subsequence/substring is a palindrome.
learn: Mirror pairs (i, n-1-i) are independent: fix each pair greedily, middle char is free when n is odd
Every palindrome of length >= 2 contains a palindrome of length 2 or 3 (useful for "no palindromic substring" tasks)
Palindromic subsequence of length 3 exists iff some value appears twice at distance >= 2
Count-based reasoning: pairs of letters build the two halves, at most one odd letter in the middle
Two-pointer shrink from both ends when you may delete one kind of character
For many substring palindrome queries move on to hashing or Manacher

subtopics.name: Subsequences & greedy matching
subtopics.summary: Check whether t is a subsequence of s by a single greedy left-to-right scan, and extend this with next-occurrence tables or prefix/suffix match arrays. Shows up in "remove characters", "minimum number of copies of s to form t", and "longest removable substring" problems.
learn: Greedy matching: take the earliest possible match of each character of t; this is optimal
Precompute nxt[i][c] = next index >= i holding c (O(26n)) or store positions per letter and binary search
pre[i] = position where t[0..i] finishes greedily from the left, suf[i] = from the right; combine them to remove a maximum substring
Counting subsequences such as "abc" uses running counts (number of a, number of ab, ...)
Substring vs subsequence: a substring is contiguous; many traps rely on mixing the two
Lexicographically largest subsequence = suffix maxima taken from right to left

subtopics.name: Lexicographic order tricks
subtopics.summary: Reason about lexicographic comparison to build the smallest/largest possible string greedily: the first differing position decides everything. Appears in "minimise the string with k operations", choosing best prefix to repeat, comparing concatenations and MEX-like strings.
learn: Greedy: make the earliest position as small as possible, then recurse on the rest
A proper prefix is smaller than the longer string; watch this edge case in comparisons
Sort strings by a+b < b+a to minimise a concatenation
The smallest string not occurring as a substring has small length (enumerate all length-1, 2, 3 strings)
Monotonic stack to delete characters for lexicographically smallest/largest result (remove duplicate letters pattern)
For fast comparison of arbitrary substrings use hashing + binary search, Z-function or suffix array (later sub-topics)

resources.title: USACO Guide: Greedy Algorithms with Sorting

subtopics.name: Bracket sequences
subtopics.summary: A regular bracket sequence has balance (opens minus closes) that never goes negative and ends at zero. Problems ask to fix, count, colour or query bracket sequences; recognise them by "(", ")" or any balanced-token structure.
learn: Prefix balance b[i]: sequence is regular iff min b >= 0 and b[n] = 0
Stack matching gives the partner of each bracket and the longest regular substring
Minimum moves to fix = how far the balance dips below zero
Range "longest regular subsequence" queries: segment tree storing (matched, open, close)
Counting regular sequences of length 2n = Catalan number; prefix-balance DP for constrained counts
Bracket sequences also map to trees / paths (+1/-1 walk), useful for constructive tasks

subtopics.name: Prefix counts & parity masks on strings
subtopics.summary: Prefix sums over characters (count of each letter, mismatches against a periodic pattern, digit sums) turn substring questions into O(1) differences. The parity-bitmask variant (bit c = parity of letter c in the prefix) counts substrings where every letter appears an even/odd number of times.
learn: cnt[c][i] = occurrences of c in s[0..i): substring counts are differences
Compare against periodic targets (RGBRGB...) via prefix mismatch counts for every shift
Good-substring counting: transform each char (e.g. digit - 1) and count equal prefix sums with a map
Parity mask: substring has all even counts iff mask[l] == mask[r]; "at most one odd" checks the 26 single-bit flips
Use arrays instead of map when the key space is small (2^26 bitset is too big: use hashing/sorting)
Combine with two pointers when constraints are monotone in the window length

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Prefix Sums
USACO Guide: More on Prefix Sums

subtopics.name: Parsing & expression evaluation
subtopics.summary: Read structured text (numbers, words, nested brackets, loops, mini-languages) and evaluate or transform it. Recursive descent or two stacks (operands + operators with precedence) evaluate arithmetic expressions; a stack of open constructs handles nesting such as loops, comments and tags. Recognised by the CF tag "expression parsing" and long input formats.
learn: Tokenise first: split into numbers, identifiers and symbols; be careful with multi-digit numbers and signs
Two-stack (shunting-yard) evaluation: apply higher-or-equal precedence operators before pushing a new one; "(" waits for ")"
Recursive descent: expr -> term {(+|-) term}, term -> factor {(*|/) factor}, factor -> number | ( expr )
Nested constructs (for/end, comments, tags) -> stack of frames holding a multiplier or depth; cap products to avoid overflow
Decode from the right when a marker follows the encoded item (e.g. two digits then 0)
Brute force over where to insert one bracket/operator, then re-evaluate in O(n): typical O(n^2) solutions
Read whole lines with getline and handle trailing spaces / empty tokens carefully

subtopics.name: Polynomial rolling hash
subtopics.summary: Map every prefix to h[i] = s[0]*p^(i-1) + ... + s[i-1] mod M so any substring hash is h[r] - h[l]*p^(r-l) in O(1). Use it whenever you need many substring equality checks: occurrences, distinct substrings, borders, overlaps when merging words.
learn: Precompute prefix hashes and powers; substring hash = (h[r] - h[l]*pw[r-l]) mod M, keep values non-negative
Choose a large prime modulus (1e9+7 / 998244353, or 2^61-1 with 128-bit multiply) and a RANDOM base chosen at runtime
Double hashing (two moduli) or mod 2^61-1 makes collisions negligible; never use natural overflow mod 2^64 (Thue-Morse anti-hash)
Birthday paradox: comparing ~10^6 hashes pairwise needs a modulus far above 10^12
Distinct substrings of a fixed length: collect hashes in a sorted vector (avoid unordered_map hacks)
Rabin-Karp: compare the pattern hash with every window hash for O(n + m) matching
Pitfall: map characters to 1..26, not 0, so that "a" and "aa" differ
2D hashing: hash every row, then hash the column of row-hashes with a second base to compare sub-matrices in O(1)

resources.title: Rolling hash and 8 interesting problems (CF blog)

subtopics.name: Collisions & anti-hash safety
subtopics.summary: Understand why hashes collide and how hackers break fixed bases, overflow (mod 2^64) hashing and unordered_map. Matters in every hackable round (Div 2/3/Educational) where a deterministic hash can be hacked after the contest.
learn: Probability of a collision for one comparison is about n/M for polynomial hashes; across many comparisons multiply by their number
mod 2^64 hashing is broken by Thue-Morse strings regardless of the base
Fixed base + fixed modulus can be attacked by tree/lattice methods: randomise the base with a time-seeded RNG
Use mod 2^61-1 or a pair of moduli; compare pairs, not sums
unordered_map with default hash can be blown up to O(n^2): use a custom splitmix64 hash or sort + unique
If a solution fails on a random-looking test only after hacks, suspect the hash

resources.title: On the mathematics behind rolling hashes and anti-hash tests
Blowing up unordered_map, and how to stop getting hacked on it

subtopics.name: Hashing + binary search (LCP, comparisons, palindromes)
subtopics.summary: Binary search the length of the longest common prefix of two substrings using O(1) hash checks, giving O(log n) lexicographic comparison of any two substrings and palindrome radius computation. Used for longest repeated / common substring (binary search on answer), sorting cyclic shifts, palindrome queries with updates.
learn: LCP(i, j) by binary search on length with hash equality: O(log n)
Compare substrings lexicographically: find LCP, then compare the next character
Hash the reversed string too: s[l..r] is a palindrome iff forward hash == backward hash
Longest substring occurring >= k times / common to two strings: binary search the length, check with a hash set
Hash in a Fenwick/segment tree supports point updates (CSES Palindrome Queries)
Combine with DP when transitions need "does block A equal block B" (e.g. word abbreviations)

subtopics.name: Set / multiset hashing (XOR & sum hashing)
subtopics.summary: Assign each value a random 64-bit number; the XOR (or sum) of a range is then a fingerprint of its set/multiset. Recognise it when you must test "every value occurs an even number of times", "these two ranges are permutations of each other" or "this subarray is a permutation" many times.
learn: XOR of random labels over a range is 0 (whp) iff every value appears an even number of times
Sum of random labels fingerprints a multiset; compare with the fingerprint of {1..k} to detect permutations
For "appears exactly k times" use labels in Z_k (sum modulo k per component) or cumulative counts mod k
Prefix XOR + hash map counts subarrays with the property in O(n)
Use mt19937_64 seeded with time; 64-bit labels make collisions practically impossible
Graph/cycle tasks: give each edge/cycle a random value and XOR along paths (Zobrist hashing)
Hash a vertex by the XOR/sum of its neighbours labels to group vertices with equal neighbourhoods
Rooted-tree hashing / isomorphism is taught in the Trees area (@trees-hashing)

resources.title: USACO Guide: String Hashing (XOR hashing section)

subtopics.name: Prefix function & KMP matching
subtopics.summary: pi[i] is the length of the longest proper border (prefix that is also a suffix) of s[0..i]. Computing it in O(n) and running it on pattern + "#" + text gives all occurrences; it is the go-to deterministic tool for borders and pattern matching.
learn: Compute pi with the "fall back j = pi[j-1]" loop; amortised O(n)
Matching: pi of p + "#" + t, positions where pi == |p| are occurrences
All borders of s are pi[n-1], pi[pi[n-1]-1], ... (chain of failure links)
Count occurrences of every prefix: cnt[pi[i]]++, then propagate down the failure chain
Number of distinct substrings in O(n^2) by adding characters one at a time
Works on arrays of integers too (e.g. differences of consecutive heights)

subtopics.name: Borders, periods & repetitions
subtopics.summary: A string has period p iff it has a border of length n - p; the smallest period is n - pi[n-1] and the string is a repetition of a block iff that period divides n. Appears in "shortest string whose repetition gives s", LCM/GCD of strings, cyclic shift cycles and necklace problems.
learn: Minimal period = n - pi[n-1]; s is k-times a block iff n % period == 0
All periods correspond to all borders (walk the failure chain)
Common divisors of two strings: divisors of gcd(|a|,|b|) that are periods of both
Repeated application of a permutation to a string: each cycle returns after its minimal period (lcm of those)
Periodicity lemma: periods p and q with p + q <= n + gcd(p, q) imply period gcd(p, q)
Hashing alternative: check s[0..n-p) == s[p..n) for each candidate p
Tandem repeats (squares ww): O(n^2) by fixing the half-length and counting equal positions at distance L; all repetitions in O(n log n) with Main-Lorentz

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Prefix function: compressing a string

subtopics.name: KMP automaton & DP over matches
subtopics.summary: Turn the prefix function into an automaton aut[state][c] (state = length of the matched prefix) and run DP over (position, automaton state) to count or optimise strings that contain / avoid a pattern. Typical for "count strings of length n containing s as a substring" and for LCS-with-forbidden-substring.
learn: aut[j][c] = j+1 if p[j] == c else aut[pi[j-1]][c]; build in O(m * alphabet)
DP state (i, j): processed i characters, currently matched j characters of the pattern
Counting strings that contain p = total - strings avoiding p (avoid state m)
Multiple patterns: use Aho-Corasick instead (same idea on a trie)
Combine with other DP dimensions (balance of brackets, LCS indices, number of occurrences)
Prefix-function queries on extended strings: memoise automaton transitions for the fixed part

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Prefix function: building an automaton

subtopics.name: Z-function & applications
subtopics.summary: z[i] is the length of the longest common prefix of s and s[i..]; it is computed in O(n) with the [l, r) window trick. Use it for matching (pattern + "$" + text), checking which prefixes occur where, comparing a string against all its suffixes, and big-number comparisons of substrings.
learn: Maintain the rightmost segment [l, r) that matches a prefix; reuse z[i - l] inside it
Matching: z of p + "$" + t, positions with z == |p|
Prefix of length k is also a suffix iff z[n-k] == k
Number of occurrences of each prefix: count z values then suffix-sum
Compare s[i..] with s lexicographically in O(1) using z[i] and the next character
Z of t + s compares every suffix of s with t; useful for splitting a number into bounded parts (DP)
Z and prefix function are interconvertible; pick whichever is more natural

subtopics.name: Trie (prefix tree)
subtopics.summary: A rooted tree where each edge is a character and each node is a prefix of some inserted string. Use it for many prefix queries, longest common prefix sums over pairs, dictionary DP (split text into words), and games played by appending letters.
learn: Array-based nodes: int nxt[N][26], cnt[N], end[N]; node count = total length + 1
Sum over pairs of LCP lengths = sum over nodes of C(cnt, 2)
Word-break DP: from each position walk down the trie (O(n * max word length))
Games on prefixes: compute win/lose on the trie bottom-up (can-win and can-lose separately)
Store the minimum/maximum index or count at every node for "first string with this prefix" queries
Memory: allocate exactly total length nodes; reset only used nodes between test cases

subtopics.name: Binary (XOR) trie
subtopics.summary: Insert numbers bit by bit from the most significant bit; walking greedily to the opposite bit answers max/min XOR with a set of numbers in O(log C). Recognise it from "maximum XOR of a pair/subarray", multiset queries with XOR, and counting pairs whose XOR is below k.
learn: Max XOR with x: at each bit try to go to child (bit of x) ^ 1
Subarray XOR = prefix[r] ^ prefix[l]: insert prefixes as you sweep
Keep a count per node to support deletion (multiset) and counting pairs with XOR < k
Global XOR updates: keep a lazy mask instead of modifying the trie; MEX after XOR walks down full subtrees
Divide-and-conquer on the trie for minimum XOR spanning tree / inversion counts per bit
Store max index per node for "latest prefix with XOR >= k" queries; persistent version for range queries

resources.title: USACO Guide: String Searching (Trie: XOR problems)

subtopics.name: Advanced XOR trie (merging, D&C, persistence)
subtopics.summary: Harder tasks build tries over subtrees or prefixes and combine them: divide and conquer over the trie for XOR-MST, tries per parity class, persistent tries for range-restricted maximum XOR, and trie walks with counts for k-th smallest XOR.
learn: XOR-MST (Boruvka on a trie): split by the highest bit, connect the two halves by one minimum XOR edge
k-th smallest pairwise XOR: walk all n pointers down the trie simultaneously bit by bit
Persistent trie: version r holds prefixes 0..r with latest-index info for max XOR in [l, r]
Separate tries by depth parity / colour when queries depend on that class
Small-to-large merging of tries over subtrees
Binary search on the answer + trie check (count pairs with XOR < mid) for k-th smallest subarray/pair values
Divide and conquer on the position of the maximum, querying a persistent trie on the smaller side

subtopics.name: Aho-Corasick automaton
subtopics.summary: Build a trie of all patterns plus suffix (failure) links by BFS to match a whole dictionary against a text in O(total length + matches). Use it for "count occurrences of each pattern in the text", "for each position how many patterns end here", and pattern-set queries.
learn: Failure link of a node = longest proper suffix that is also a trie node; compute by BFS
Goto transitions go[v][c] turn the trie into a full automaton
Count occurrences of each pattern: add 1 to the visited state, then accumulate along suffix links in reverse BFS order
Patterns ending at a position = sum of terminal counts along the output-link chain (precompute in BFS)
Number of distinct pattern lengths is O(sqrt(total length)) - useful bound
Suffix-link tree + Euler tour + Fenwick handles dynamic pattern sets and online queries
Dynamic insertions: binary-grouping (log n automata) technique

subtopics.name: DP on the Aho-Corasick automaton
subtopics.summary: Run DP over (length, automaton state [, extra mask]) to count or optimise strings with respect to a set of patterns; with fixed small state count, matrix exponentiation handles huge lengths. Recognise from "count strings of length n that contain none / all of these words" or "maximise happiness from occurring pickup lines".
learn: State = node of the automaton; value of a state = sum of terminal values along suffix links
Forbidden patterns: mark nodes whose suffix-link chain contains a terminal as dead
Must contain all patterns: add a bitmask of seen patterns (small number of patterns)
Large n: (max,+) or (+,*) matrix exponentiation over the automaton states
Question marks / wildcards: transition over all letters, combine with bitmask DP on the letters used

subtopics.name: Manacher's algorithm
subtopics.summary: Computes the radius of the longest palindrome centred at every position (odd and even) in O(n) by reusing a mirrored centre inside the rightmost palindrome. Use it for longest palindromic substring, counting palindromic substrings, and "longest palindromic prefix/suffix" questions.
learn: Handle even centres by inserting separators (s = "#a#b#") or keep two arrays d1/d2
Rightmost palindrome [l, r]: start from min(r - i, d[l + r - i]) and extend naively
Number of palindromic substrings = sum of radii
Longest palindromic prefix: largest centre whose palindrome touches index 0
Palindromes starting/ending at each index: difference arrays over the radii
Hashing + binary search gives the same radii in O(n log n) when Manacher is awkward
For n <= 5000 the O(n^2) table pal[l][r] (or expand around every centre) is often enough

resources.title: Manacher's algorithm and code readability (CF blog)

subtopics.name: Palindromic tree (eertree)
subtopics.summary: The eertree stores every distinct palindromic substring as a node (at most n + 2) with suffix links to the longest palindromic suffix. It answers counts of distinct palindromes, occurrences of each palindrome and powers palindromic-factorisation DP via series links.
learn: Two roots: length -1 (imaginary) and length 0; add characters one by one, at most one new node each
Suffix link = longest proper palindromic suffix; occurrences via reverse-order accumulation
Palindromic factorisation in O(n log n) using diff/series links (lengths form O(log n) arithmetic progressions)
Count palindromes ending at each position = depth in the suffix-link tree
Palindrome pair counting (Palisection) also solvable with Manacher + prefix sums

resources.title: Palindromic tree: behind the scenes (adamant, CF blog)
USACO Guide: String Suffix Structures (Palindromic Tree)

subtopics.name: Suffix array
subtopics.summary: Sort all suffixes (or cyclic shifts) by prefix doubling in O(n log n) (or O(n log^2 n) with std::sort). Once built, pattern search is a binary search, and sorted order exposes lexicographic structure: k-th substring, minimal shift, BWT.
learn: Prefix doubling: rank pairs (rank[i], rank[i + 2^k]) and re-sort; counting sort gives O(n log n)
Append a sentinel smaller than all characters (or work with cyclic shifts)
Pattern occurrence = contiguous range of the SA, found by two binary searches: O(m log n)
Concatenate several strings with distinct separators to compare them together
Same doubling idea sorts strings defined by XOR/shift operations
Burrows-Wheeler transform and its inverse are SA applications (CSES String Transform)

subtopics.name: LCP array & applications
subtopics.summary: Kasai's algorithm builds lcp[i] = LCP of adjacent suffixes in the SA in O(n); with a sparse table, LCP of any two suffixes is a range minimum. Classic uses: number of distinct substrings, longest repeated / common substring, counting substrings occurring k times, sums of LCP over sets of suffixes.
learn: Kasai: process suffixes in text order, lcp decreases by at most 1 each step
Distinct substrings = n(n+1)/2 - sum(lcp)
LCP(sa_i, sa_j) = min(lcp[i+1..j]): sparse table for O(1) queries
Longest common substring of A and B: adjacent SA entries from different strings in A + "#" + B
Sum of pairwise LCPs over a set: sort by SA rank, monotonic stack or DSU merging by decreasing lcp
Substrings occurring >= k times: sliding window minimum over lcp

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Suffix Array: LCP and applications

subtopics.name: Suffix automaton & suffix tree
subtopics.summary: The suffix automaton is the minimal DFA recognising all suffixes (at most 2n states), built online in O(n); its suffix-link tree is the suffix tree of the reversed string. It answers substring membership, number of distinct substrings, occurrences of every substring and k-th lexicographic substring.
learn: Each state = class of substrings with the same endpos set; len[v] and link[v] determine it
Online extension with cloning; total states <= 2n - 1, transitions <= 3n - 4
Distinct substrings = sum(len[v] - len[link[v]]); occurrences = endpos sizes via the link tree
k-th substring: count paths from each state (DP on DAG) and walk
Generalised SAM for several strings; longest common substring by running the second string through
Suffix tree (Ukkonen or from SA + LCP) is the dual structure; pick whichever you know best

resources.title: A short guide to suffix automata (CF blog)

subtopics.name: DP powered by string tools (LCP table, palindrome table, matching)
subtopics.summary: DP over positions or substrings whose transitions ask string questions: "are these two blocks equal?", "is s[l..r] a palindrome?", "which substring is larger?", "where does t occur?". Precompute the answers with an O(n^2) LCP table, a palindrome table, hashing, Z or KMP so each transition is O(1). Classic DP forms (LCS, edit distance, subsequence counting) live in the DP area (@dp-lcs-edit, @dp-strings).
learn: O(n^2) LCP table: lcp[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] ? lcp[i+1][j+1] + 1 : 0, filled from the back (use short/int16 to save memory)
Compare two substrings of equal length via lcp: equal iff lcp >= len, otherwise compare the first different character
Palindrome table pal[l][r] = s[l]==s[r] && pal[l+1][r-1]; prefix sums of palindromes ending/starting at i count pairs
Splitting into increasing numbers: dp[i][len] with LCP-based comparison of the previous block plus suffix sums
Compression DP: dp[i] = min over j of dp[j] + cost(s[j..i)), where the period of every substring comes from a prefix function started at j
Find all occurrences first (KMP/Z/hash), then DP over occurrences (cover / remove all occurrences with minimum moves and count ways)
Memory: n = 5000 gives 25M cells; reuse rows or store only what transitions need

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Prefix function: compressing a string

subtopics.name: Cyclic strings: minimal rotation & Lyndon factorisation
subtopics.summary: Duval's algorithm splits a string into a non-increasing sequence of Lyndon words in O(n); the lexicographically smallest cyclic shift is found with it (or with Booth's algorithm / SA on s+s). Appears in canonical forms of cyclic strings and necklaces, and greedy "cut and reverse" tasks.
learn: Lyndon word: strictly smaller than all its proper rotations
Duval: maintain i, j, k pointers; O(n) time, O(1) memory
Minimal rotation: run Duval on s + s; the answer is the start of the last Lyndon factor that begins before position n
Alternatives: suffix array of s + s, or hashing + binary search comparisons in O(n log n)
Canonical form of a cyclic string = its minimal rotation (compare necklaces by it, count distinct rotations)
Booth's algorithm (failure function on s + s) is an O(n) alternative to Duval

subtopics.name: Matching with FFT / bitsets (wildcards, mismatches)
subtopics.summary: When the pattern has wildcards or you need, for every alignment, the number of matching characters, encode the comparison as a convolution (sum over (a - b)^2 * a * b with 0 for wildcards) and use FFT; for small alphabets do one convolution per letter. Bitset shift-and gives O(nm/64) substring queries.
learn: Exact matching with wildcards: sum p_j t_{i+j} (p_j - t_{i+j})^2 = 0 expands into three convolutions
Per-letter indicator convolutions count matches for each shift (alphabet size times FFT)
Approximate matching (within distance k): blur the text indicator first, then convolve
Bitset shift-and: occ &= (pos[c] >> j) for each pattern character; supports point updates
Use NTT or double precision carefully; reverse one of the sequences to turn correlation into convolution

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Fast Fourier transform (string matching section)
USACO Guide: Introduction to Fast Fourier Transform
